articles.title: Registration is now full for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp
articles.content:
The demand for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp was far beyond our expectations, and we reached our maximum registration of 30 people within one day. We already have a waiting list of over 30 people, so we have closed the registration site.

We realize that this is very disappointing to many people. We hope to offer another workshop like this next summer, or possibly earlier.

If you would like to get announcements about upcoming boot camps and webinars, you should join our email list.

You may also consider hosting a Mini ERP Boot Camp at your institution (in person or over Zoom).
articles.author: Steve Luck

articles.title: New Paper: Using Multivariate Pattern Analysis to Increase Effect Sizes for ERP Amplitude Comparisons
articles.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Bahle, B., Simmons, A. M., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses. Psychophysiology, 61, e14570. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14570 [preprint]

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be used to “decode” subtle information from ERP signals, such as which of several faces a participant is perceiving or the orientation that someone is holding in working memory (see this previous blog post). This approach is so powerful that we started wondering whether it might also give us greater statistical power in more typical experiments where the goal is to determine whether an ERP component differs in amplitude across experimental conditions. For example, might we more easily be able to tell if N400 amplitude is different between two different classes of words by using decoding? If so, that might make it possible to detect effects that would otherwise be too small to be significant.

To address this question, we compared decoding with the conventional ERP analysis approach with using the 6 experimental paradigms in the ERP CORE. In the conventional ERP analysis, we measured the mean amplitude during the standard measurement window from each participant in the two conditions of the paradigm (e.g., faces versus cars for N170, deviants versus standards for MMN). We quantified the magnitude of the difference between conditions using Cohen’s dz (the variant of Cohen’s d corresponding to a paired t test). For example, the effect size in the conventional ERP comparison of faces versus cars in the N170 paradigm was approximately 1.7 (see the figure).

We also applied decoding to each paradigm. For example, in the N170 paradigm, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between ERPs elicited by faces and ERPs elicited by cars. This was done separately for each subject, and we converted the decoding accuracy into Cohen’s dz so that it could be compared with the dz from the conventional ERP analysis. As you can see from the bar labeled SVM in the figure above, the effect size for the SVM-based decoding analysis was almost twice as large as the effect size for the conventional ERP analysis. That’s a huge difference!

We found a similar benefit for SVM-based decoding over conventional ERP analyses in 7 of the 10 cases we tested (see the figure below). In the other 3 cases, the ERP and SVM effects were approximately equivalent. So, there doesn’t seem to be a downside to using decoding, at least in terms of effect size. But there can be a big benefit.

Because decoding has many possible benefits, we’ve added it into ERPLAB Toolbox. It’s super easy to use, and we’ve created detailed documentation and a video to explain how it works at a conceptual level and to show you how to use it.

We encourage you to apply it to your own data. It may give you the power to detect effects that are too small to be detected with conventional ERP analyses.

articles.content:
Publication date: 1 January 2027

Source: Brain Research, Volume 1894

Author(s): Fashwa Khan Tareen, Sana Javaid, Waseem Ashraf, Syed Muhammad Muneeb Anjum, Rana Muhammad Zahid Mushtaq, Asad Abrar, Faleh Alqahtani, Imran Imran

articles.title: An Information Compass for Probabilistic Reasoning in the Brain
articles.content: Probabilistic reasoning in the brain has been studied primarily using simple two-choice tasks that are experimentally and theoretically tractable but have unclear relevance to more complex problems. Here we generalize principles from these studies using information geometry, which treats probability distributions (``beliefs'') as points on statistical manifolds whose geometry captures relationships between those beliefs. We introduce an ``information compass,'' a context-dependent, one-dimensional axis along which an arbitrarily complex belief is reinforced or repudiated. Projecting high-dimensional belief updates onto this axis casts even complex decisions into familiar forms of deliberation and commitment used for simpler decisions. Our framework provides a unified account of how biological and artificial systems can use geometric forms of probabilistic reasoning to make decisions across a range of tasks and domains.
articles.author: Bosulu, J., Balasubramanian, V., Kilpatrick, Z. P., Josic, K., Gold, J. I.

articles.title: Selective Nerve Block of A- or C-Afferents Confirms Dual Role in Touch Pleasantness but Not Touch-Pain Modulation
articles.content: Gentle and deep pressure are distinct types of touch that often elicit pleasant sensations and modulate pain. Although touch pleasantness has traditionally been attributed to unmyelinated C-tactile afferents, growing evidence suggests an important contribution of myelinated A-fibers. However, the relative role of A- and C-fibers in touch-evoked pleasantness and pain modulation remains unclear. To test the role of A- and C-fibers in touch pleasantness, healthy adults underwent selective peripheral nerve block of the superficial radial nerve to preferentially impair either A- or C-fiber function. Touch pleasantness of brushing (Study 1; N = 24) or deep pressure (Study 2; N = 24) and touch-induced modulation of heat pain were assessed before and after the nerve block. Both nerve blocks significantly reduced the perceived pleasantness of both gentle brushing and deep pressure, supporting a substantial contribution of myelinated A-fibers and well as unmyelinated C-fibers (presumably C-tactile fibers) to affective touch. In addition, block of A-fibers did not diminish touch-induced modulation of experimental heat pain, suggesting a particular pain-inhibiting role for C-tactile fibers. These findings supply causal evidence in healthy adults that myelinated A-fibers are highly involved in touch pleasantness-alongside C-tactile fibers-but are not involved in touch-induced pain relief.
articles.author: Albinni, B., Crankshaw, L. N., Jones, E., Alasha, V., Zimmerman, M., Schuster, N., Said, E., Strigo, I., Case, L. K.

articles.title: Short-term cortical stimulation combined with targeted rehabilitation and Chondroitinase ABC improves upper limb function following a cervical contusion injury
articles.content: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) at the cervical level can lead to permanent upper limb and hand motor impairments, thus restoring upper limb function is amongst the highest priorities for SCI patients and can have extensive effects on improving quality of life and patient independence. We previously showed that long-term cortical stimulation of the motor cortex (10 weeks) when applied in conjunction with a daily upper limb targeted rehabilitation regiment and a neuroplasticity enhancing therapy such as lentiviral Chondroitinase ABC (ChABC) can lead to an increase of muscle activity which was translated to restored skilled function after a clinically relevant contusion injury. Here, we investigate the effects of a short term cortical stimulation protocol as part of the same neurorehabilitation paradigm to asses its efficecy. Adult rats were implanted unilaterally with stimulating electrodes (contralaterally to the dominant forepaw as determined by skilled reaching) on the surface of the motor cortex and received a bilateral cervical (C5/C6) contusion injury to produce severe and long lasting forelimb motor deficits. Contused animals received acute intraspinal injections of the neuroplasticity promoting agent ChABC and 12 consecutives days of epidural electrical stimulation of the motor cortex along with daily targeted upper limb behavioural rehabilitation (Whishaw Window and Montoya staircase, 15 minutes for 5 days/week for 7 weeks) starting at 7 days post injury. Our results revealed marked improvements in the tasks specific for assessing upper limb dexterity. These were also corroborated by electrophysiological and anatomical evidence. Thus, we provide robust evidence that short term cortical epidural stimulation as part of a combinational neurorehabilitation paradigm can restore upper limb function after a cervical contusion.
articles.author: sinopoulou, e., Burnside, E. R., Bartus, K., Bradbury, E. J.

articles.title: The Cost to Scroll: Short-form Video Use and Episodic Memory
articles.content: Short-form video platforms expose users to rapid streams of novel content; these features are posited to place heavy demands on cognitive processes. In a preregistered online study, we used device-reported screen time to examine whether short-form video use is associated with sustained attention and episodic memory in participants aged 18-24 yrs (N = 502). During a sustained attention task, participants made indoor/outdoor decisions on scene stimuli, with 90% frequent trials and 10% infrequent trials; the subsequent surprise recognition test assessed memory for these items. Among participants with device-reported TikTok or Instagram use (N = 398), short-form video use was not associated with attention performance. By contrast, greater short-form video use was associated with poorer episodic memory; this relationship was driven by poorer recognition of infrequent-category items. These findings connect heavier short-form video consumption with poorer episodic memory in young adults, showing how daily digital habits co-vary with memory function.
articles.author: Chen, K. K., Miller, D. S., Nguyen, K. K., Wagner, A. D., Tran, T. T.

articles.title: Critical scaling of cortical ensembles without cooperative amplification
articles.content: Cortical neurons are sparsely and weakly connected, motivating the long-standing idea that they must act collectively, as cell assemblies, to exert substantial influence on surrounding networks. Yet a few spikes in a single pyramidal neuron can recruit thousands of cortical neurons according to a power law with exponent ~0.285, consistent with a two-dimensional system near a critical percolation transition. Here we holographically stimulated ensembles of 1 to 16 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in visual cortex of awake mice while imaging hundreds of neighbouring neurons. Across two orders of magnitude in evoked spike count, network responses followed the same scaling law observed for single-neuron perturbations, with no detectable threshold at which co-activation produced additional amplification. Recruitment was sublinear, suppression increased with ensemble size, and ongoing scale-free avalanche dynamics remained stationary. Nevertheless, ensemble identity became increasingly decodable from surrounding activity. Thus, coordinated firing increases representational specificity without escaping the critical dynamics governing propagation: cortical ensembles convey identity without gaining disproportionate causal impact.
articles.author: Ribeiro, T. L., Siddiqui, R., Gifford, B., Pajevic, S., Plenz, D.

articles.title: Real-time posterior probabilistic TMS motor mapping with robust individualized stopping criteria
articles.content: Background. Electric-field-informed regression provides high-resolution transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) motor maps, but conventional nonlinear fitting is too slow to update the map during acquisition, so sessions rely on predefined stimulation budgets, despite substantial inter-individual variability in the data required for stable localization. Objective. To develop a real-time analysis updating a posterior probability map between pulses and compare its hotspots with finger-tapping functional MRI (fMRI). Methods. We analyzed two independent cohorts (12 and 13 participants, one newly collected), analyzing each hand muscle independently. We replaced the conventional per-element sigmoid fit with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and transformed the resulting score map into a posterior probability map using marginal-likelihood evidence. Acquisition stopped once posterior mass within 5 mm of the hotspot passed a preset confidence level. Results. The Spearman and linear scores updated the region of interest within milliseconds, versus tens of seconds for sigmoid fitting. Spearman more closely matched the full-data sigmoid hotspot in recorded sessions and converged faster and more precisely to the true source in virtual subjects. Across both fast scores, at a confidence level of 0.85, the stopping criterion was met after a median of 74-159 pulses, with 26-454 across individual problems. FDI hotspots lay 8.3 {+/-} 4.3 mm from the fMRI center of gravity, in the precentral hand region. Conclusions. Rank correlation reduces computation time without loss of accuracy relative to sigmoid fitting. The resulting posterior probability map provides a session-specific stopping criterion in place of a fixed pulse budget.
articles.author: Qiu, R., Feng, Z.-J., Numssen, O., Zang, Y.-F., Wilhelmy, F., Güresir, E., Knösche, T. R., Weise, K.

articles.title: AMPK-dependent brain-wide norepinephrine release promotes recovery from metabolic coma in mice
articles.content: Coma is a pathological brain state characterized by loss of consciousness. How the brain recovers from coma remains largely unknown. Using mouse models of metabolic coma, we identified an endogenous neuromodulatory pathway that actively promotes coma recovery. In mice subjected to hypoglycemic coma, hypoglycemia triggered AMPK-dependent excitation of nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) neurons, which activated locus coeruleus (LC) norepinephrine neurons through a glutamatergic NTS-LC circuit. LC activation drives widespread norepinephrine release across cortical and subcortical regions, thereby promoting post-coma arousal. Notably, coma-associated brain-wide norepinephrine release was unconventional in both scale and duration, with a magnitude approximately 10-fold higher than physiological norepinephrine release during sleep-wake cycles. This neuromodulatory process also operated during hypercapnic coma. Vagus nerve stimulation accelerated coma recovery by engaging this endogenous anti-coma mechanism. Our findings uncover an AMPK-dependent brainstem circuit that actively restores arousal from metabolic coma, revealing a neural defense strategy against profound metabolic stress.
articles.author: Wu, M., Zhang, L., Li, Y., Chen, G., Li, D., Zhao, M., Gu, H., Song, H., Cao, Y., Yang, Z., Liu, Z., Zhang, F., Li, T.-Z., Miao, H.-H., Cao, P.

articles.title: Computational Evaluation of tDCS Montage Separability and Dose Coverage for Practice-Specific Mindfulness Experiments
articles.content: A practice-specific stimulation experiment requires candidate montages that differ in regional electric-field exposure without sacrificing interpretable target dose. We evaluated this requirement for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages intended to test focused-attention and open-monitoring mindfulness practices. Four focused-attention candidates and six open-monitoring candidates formed 24 pairs, evaluated with SimNIBS 4.6 in 20 existing anatomical head models at a linearly scaled current of 2 mA. Outcomes were regional 99th-percentile field magnitude, a normalized double-dissociation index (DDI), suprathreshold overlap, and individual dose coverage. Eighteen pairs passed four recorded progression criteria, but only five also met a post hoc requirement that both intended regional contrasts be positive in at least 80% of heads. A positive DDI alone concealed a reversed salience-region contrast in one conventional comparison. The nominated F3-centered 4-by-1 ring paired with F8-Fp2 sponges (FA-05 x OM-02) produced both directional preferences in 20/20 heads, with median DDI 1.561 and median suprathreshold Dice 0.000. The conventional F3-Fp2 and FT8-FCz sponge pair (FA-02 x OM-07) produced both preferences in 19/20 heads, with DDI 0.627 and Dice 0.186. Both anatomical targets reached the operational 0.20 V/m floor in 11/20 versus 20/20 heads, respectively. ROAST 4.0, with ring placement held fixed, supported both nominations but exposed dose disagreement. Across conductivity sensitivity draws, directional separability persisted more consistently than absolute dose. These results establish a regional separability-dose trade-off within the tested candidate set and show why a summed contrast cannot substitute for a directional conjunction. They support selection of a discriminating experiment, not whole-network selectivity, physiological efficacy, or a validated treatment.
articles.author: Bruschi, D. L., Schiavi, A., Joseph, I.

articles.title: Braintree: An agentic framework for in-silico vision neuroscience
articles.content: Vision neuroscience has many of the ingredients needed to conduct experiments entirely in-silico. We need AI systems that can reason over scientific knowledge, generative methods for creating precisely controlled stimuli, image-computable models that can predict neural responses with increasing accuracy, and tools that can analyze and interpret data. Here we take the first step toward making a vision neuroscience experiment end-to-end computable. We introduce Braintree, an agentic framework that can autonomously run multi-experiment studies directly with in-silico models of human visual cortex. Given a hypothesis, Braintree can reason over the current literature, design an experiment, build a stimulus set from algorithmically manipulated or synthesized stimuli, run the experiment on candidate brain encoding models, analyze the responses and then use the results to design even stronger tests. The entire loop runs autonomously and can accept human input at any stage. We evaluated Braintree on three increasingly open-ended scientific problems. First, Braintree reproduced published findings using their original stimuli and then asked whether the same effects could be replicated with entirely new stimulus sets that it constructed. Second, it designed new experiments to find stimulus dimensions that could drive two brain regions differently, even when those regions otherwise had similar response profiles. Third, it searched for experiments that could tell competing models of the same brain region apart. Experiments discovered using just two models also exposed differences across a much broader set of models, suggesting that Braintree had found more general dimensions along which brain models disagree. Braintree can augment the capabilities of a vision neuroscientist as a verifier for existing hypotheses, a test-bed for new ideas, and/or a tool for generating stimuli that can discriminate between competing hypotheses or models of the brain. Braintree shows how AI agents and brain models can work together to make in-silico vision neuroscience experiment computable, allowing vision scientists to explore many more experiment conditions and identify the most informative ones to test on the human brain.
articles.author: Deb, M., Wang, R., Dipani, A., Ratan Murty, N. A.

articles.title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
articles.content: The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2-PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT-gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K current; conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na current; current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target.
articles.author: Zhao, B., Li, M., Yi, L., Li, J.

articles.author: McKeon, P.

articles.title: Functional brain activity in cancer-related cognitive impairment: a scoping review of EEG studies
articles.content: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) is reported across the cancer trajectory, yet its neurobiological basis remains incompletely understood. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a temporally precise method for assessing brain activity at rest and during cognitive processing, but its application in CRCI research has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review characterized how EEG has been used to study cognitive functioning in people with cancer, including populations studied, EEG paradigms and analytic approaches employed, and cognitive outcomes assessed. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to February 2025 for studies using EEG to examine cognitive functioning. Sixty articles were included. Most were small and cross-sectional, with publication output increasing markedly after 2015. Task-based event-related potentials, particularly from oddball and attention tasks, were used most frequently, whereas quantitative EEG approaches, including spectral power and connectivity analyses, were less common. In populations with cancers outside the central nervous system (CNS), longer P300 latency and lower amplitude were common, but opposite and null findings also occurred. Evidence from primary CNS and other intracranial tumor populations was sparse. Across cancer contexts, quantitative EEG findings showed limited convergence across articles. Associations between EEG measures and cognitive outcomes were inconsistent and often not tested directly. Overall, EEG provides a complementary approach to investigating cognition in people with cancer, but the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. Larger longitudinal studies, more consistent cognitive outcome selection, and closer integration of neural and cognitive measures are needed to establish reproducible findings and evaluate their potential clinical utility.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251084951.
articles.author: Lisa Lyngsie Hjalgrim

articles.title: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation
articles.content: Advances in naturalistic language assessment, portable neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and brain-network modeling are creating new opportunities to evaluate post-stroke aphasia under conditions closer to real-world communication. Conventional aphasia batteries and isolated linguistic tasks remain essential for diagnosis, severity classification, and treatment planning, but they provide limited information about how language-network activity supports communication in dynamic, naturalistic contexts. This integrative review, informed by a structured literature search and descriptive thematic mapping, synthesizes evidence on connected speech, discourse production, narrative comprehension, interactive communication, and contextual reading after stroke. We examine how multilevel features from these behaviors can be organized into graded, interacting dimensions of lexical-semantic access, phonological encoding, grammatical organization, discourse processing, executive-predictive control, and speech-motor output. We further review multimodal evidence from fNIRS, fMRI, EEG/ERP, lesion-symptom mapping, structural connectivity, and functional connectivity, highlighting residual left-hemisphere language networks, conditional right-hemisphere support, bilateral reorganization, domain-general control systems, and longitudinal recovery. Portable EEG and fNIRS are considered complementary approaches for repeated assessment during less constrained language tasks, with distinct temporal, spatial, and practical trade-offs. Building on this evidence, we propose an operational ecological biomarker framework that links task choice, multilevel feature extraction, multivariate behavioral profiles, neural measures, prespecified clinical questions, and longitudinal outcomes. This framework may support recovery prediction, rehabilitation stratification, neuromodulation target selection, individualized therapy planning, and monitoring of functional communication.
articles.author: Yulong Bai

articles.title: Hierarchical affective predictive imbalance in adolescent borderline personality disorder: task-evoked fMRI evidence from multimodal machine learning
articles.content: BackgroundPredictive-processing accounts of BPD, including the hierarchical-prior-imbalance account proposed by Herzog, offer a framework for interpreting affective instability and impulsivity. The present task-fMRI study evaluates whether discriminative task-evoked patterns are consistent with this framework; because it does not directly estimate prediction errors, precision weighting, or hierarchical belief updating, it is not a mechanistic test of predictive processing.MethodsTo evaluate this question, this study developed a leakage-controlled multimodal machine learning framework for individualized classification of adolescents with BPD and healthy controls based on emotional Go/No-Go task-fMRI activity. Three feature domains were constructed: functional connectivity (FC), task-evoked general linear model (GLM)-derived temporal features, and clinical variables. Seven feature settings, including single-modality, dual-modality, and full multimodal combinations, were evaluated using multiple conventional machine learning classifiers, including logistic regression, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, Gaussian naive Bayes, multilayer perceptron, random forest, and XGBoost or gradient boosting.ResultsThe results showed that task-evoked GLM-derived features provided the strongest single-modality discriminative information (AUC of 0.881 ± 0.055). SHAP analysis confirmed the predominance of GLM-derived features, accounting for 83.1% of total model attribution, compared to 9.5 and 7.5% for functional connectivity and clinical variables, respectively. At the neural level, discriminative features were distributed across visual/perceptual regions (calcarine, cuneus, occipital cortex), temporoparietal/default-mode hubs (angular and supramarginal gyri), frontal control regions (inferior frontal gyrus), and subcortical structures (putamen). This distributed pattern aligns with a hierarchical organization spanning perceptual input, contextual/self-referential processing, and top-down inhibitory control systems, consistent with the proposed model of hierarchical affective predictive imbalance.ConclusionTask-evoked GLM-derived features were the primary source of discriminative information for adolescent BPD, with functional connectivity and clinical variables providing modest additional value. The resulting classification pattern is consistent with hierarchical predictive-processing accounts but does not establish a specific predictive-processing mechanism. The same regional pattern may also reflect visual attention, salience processing, and executive inhibitory control.
